name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Staining of xylem and phloem in stem

questiontext.text: A transverse section of stem is stained first with safranin and then with fast green following the usual schedule of double staining for the preparation of a permanent slide. What would be the colour of the stained xylem and phloem?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Double staining of plant anatomical sections uses two contrasting dyes that bind selectively to different cell wall components: safranin and fast green.

Step 2: Evaluation of Tissue Wall Composition
Safranin is a basic dye that specifically stains lignified, suberised, and cutinised cell walls red or pink. Xylem elements (such as tracheids, vessels, and xylem fibres) possess thick lignified secondary cell walls. Fast green is an acidic dye that stains cellulosic primary cell walls green. Phloem elements (such as sieve tubes, companion cells, and phloem parenchyma) have unlignified cellulosic cell walls.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Upon double staining with safranin followed by fast green, the lignified xylem appears red and the cellulosic phloem appears green. Therefore, the colour of the stained xylem and phloem would be red and green.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCHING_Q02 - Matching plant tissues with their functions

questiontext.text: Match the following plant tissues with their corresponding functions or features.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant tissues are classified into meristematic and permanent tissues (simple, complex, and tissue systems) based on their capacity for division, cell wall structure, and specialised functions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
Meristematic tissue consists of undifferentiated, actively dividing cells responsible for plant growth. Parenchyma is a living simple tissue with thin cellulosic walls that performs photosynthesis (chlorenchyma) and storage of food. Collenchyma is a living mechanical tissue with unevenly thickened walls that provides mechanical support to growing stems and petioles. Sclerenchyma consists of dead, thick-walled lignified cells comprising fibres and sclereids. The epidermal tissue system forms the outermost protective covering and contains stomata for gaseous exchange and transpiration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matches are: Meristem with actively dividing cells; Parenchyma with photosynthesis, storage; Collenchyma with mechanical support; Sclerenchyma with sclereids; and Epidermal tissue with stomata.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCHING_Q03 - Matching epidermal structures with their features

questiontext.text: Match the following plant structures with their characteristic features.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The epidermal tissue system of plants includes the epidermis, cuticle, stomata, and specialised epidermal cells such as bulliform cells.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
The cuticle is a waxy thick layer deposited on the outside of the epidermis of aerial parts to prevent water loss. Bulliform cells are large, empty, colourless cells found in the adaxial epidermis of grasses that help roll leaves inward during water stress. Stomata are pores enclosed by two bean-shaped or dumb-bell-shaped guard cells that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. The epidermis is typically a single-layered outermost protective covering of the primary plant body.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matches are: Cuticle with waxy layer; Bulliform cells with empty colourless cell; Stomata with guard cells; and Epidermis with single layer.

questiontext.text: Identify the simple tissue system from the following

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Permanent tissues in plants are classified into simple tissues (made of only one type of cells similar in structure and function) and complex tissues (made of more than one type of cells working together as a unit).

Step 2: Evaluation of Options
Parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma are simple permanent tissues. Xylem and phloem are complex permanent tissues composed of multiple cell types (such as tracheids, vessels, fibres, and parenchyma in xylem; sieve elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, and phloem fibres in phloem). Epidermis is part of the epidermal tissue system rather than a simple tissue.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Among the given choices, parenchyma is a simple tissue.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Living mechanical tissue with angular thickening

questiontext.text: Cells of this tissue are living and show angular wall thickening. They also provide mechanical support. The tissue is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Simple permanent tissues differ in cell viability, wall composition, and pattern of wall thickening.

Step 2: Evaluation of Tissue Characteristics
Collenchyma consists of living cells whose cell walls are much thickened at the corners (angular thickening) due to the deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin. It provides mechanical support to the growing parts of the plant such as young stems and petioles of leaves. In contrast, sclerenchyma and most xylem elements are dead at maturity, while the epidermis primarily serves a protective role.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The living tissue with angular wall thickening that provides mechanical support is collenchyma.

Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The outermost protective layer of the primary plant body is part of the epidermal tissue system.

Step 2: Evaluation of Root Anatomy
In roots, the outermost single-layered covering composed of thin-walled living cells (many of which protrude as unicellular root hairs) is called the epiblema (also known as rhizodermis or piliferous layer). It occupies the same outermost position and serves the analogous protective and absorptive surface role as the epidermis in stems and leaves. Pericycle and endodermis are internal layers, and stele refers to all tissues inside the endodermis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Epiblema of roots is equivalent to the epidermis.

questiontext.text: A conjoint and open vascular bundle will be observed in the transverse section of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vascular bundles are classified as radial (xylem and phloem on different radii) or conjoint (xylem and phloem situated along the same radius). Conjoint bundles are further classified as open (cambium present between xylem and phloem) or closed (cambium absent).

Step 2: Evaluation of Plant Organs
Roots (both monocot and dicot) possess radial vascular bundles. Monocot stems possess conjoint and closed vascular bundles because they lack intrafascicular cambium and do not undergo secondary growth. Dicot stems possess conjoint and open vascular bundles arranged in a ring, with cambium present between the phloem and xylem to enable secondary growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A conjoint and open vascular bundle is observed in the transverse section of a dicot stem.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Formation of secondary meristems by dedifferentiation

questiontext.text: Interfascicular cambium and cork cambium are formed due to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Differentiated permanent plant cells that have lost the capacity to divide can regain the ability to divide mitotically under certain conditions; this phenomenon is termed dedifferentiation.

Step 2: Application to Secondary Meristems
During secondary growth in dicot stems, cells of the medullary rays (permanent parenchyma cells) adjoining the intrafascicular cambium become meristematic and form the interfascicular cambium. Similarly, parenchymatous cells of the outer cortex become meristematic to form the cork cambium (phellogen). Both are examples of secondary meristems arising from permanent cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Interfascicular cambium and cork cambium are formed due to cell dedifferentiation.

Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During secondary growth in the extrastelar region, a protective tissue system called periderm is formed, consisting of phellogen, phellem, and phelloderm.

Step 2: Evaluation of Terms
Phellogen is the cork cambium, a meristematic layer that divides to cut off cells on both sides. The outer cells differentiate into cork or phellem (impervious to water due to suberin deposition), while the inner cells differentiate into secondary cortex or phelloderm.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Phellogen and phellem respectively denote cork cambium and cork.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q10 - Absence of epidermis in apical meristems

questiontext.text: In which of the following pairs of parts of a flowering plant is epidermis absent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The epidermis is a differentiated permanent tissue that develops from the protoderm behind the zone of active cell division.

Step 2: Evaluation of Plant Parts
At the root tip and shoot tip, the tissue consists of actively dividing meristematic cells (root apical meristem and shoot apical meristem). Because these regions are undifferentiated meristems, a mature differentiated epidermis is absent. In contrast, shoot buds, floral buds, ovules, seeds, petioles, and pedicels possess differentiated epidermal coverings.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Epidermis is absent in the root tip and shoot tip.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q11 - Number of shoot apical meristems on twig

questiontext.text: How many shoot apical meristems are likely to be present in a twig of a plant possessing 4 branches and 26 leaves?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A plant twig possesses 4 branches and 26 leaves.

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
A shoot apical meristem (SAM) is located at the growing tip of the main stem axis and at the tip of every lateral branch. Leaves are determinate lateral appendages formed from leaf primordia and do not possess shoot apical meristems at their tips.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Number of shoot apical meristems on the main twig apex \(= 1\).
Number of shoot apical meristems on the 4 branch apices \(= 4\).
Total number of shoot apical meristems \(= 1 + 4 = 5\).

Step 4: Final Answer
There are 5 shoot apical meristems likely to be present in the twig.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q12 - Absence of vessels in gymnosperm wood

questiontext.text: A piece of wood having no vessels (trachea) must belong to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The presence of vessels (tracheae) in xylem is a characteristic feature of angiosperms, whereas gymnosperms generally lack vessels in their xylem.

Step 2: Evaluation of Organisms
Teak, mango, and palm are angiosperms and therefore possess vessels in their xylem. Pine (Pinus) is a gymnosperm (conifer), and its wood (softwood) is non-porous because it lacks vessels and consists predominantly of tracheids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A piece of wood having no vessels must belong to Pine.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q13 - Hemicellulose and pectin in collenchyma cell wall

questiontext.text: A plant tissue, when stained, showed the presence of hemicellulose and pectin in cell wall of its cells. The tissue represents

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different plant tissues have characteristic cell wall chemical compositions suited to their functions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Tissue Wall Composition
Collenchyma cells have primary cell walls thickened at the corners due to heavy deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin. Sclerenchyma and xylem elements have heavily lignified secondary cell walls, while meristematic cells have thin primary cellulosic walls without prominent pectin and hemicellulose corner thickenings.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The tissue showing prominent presence of hemicellulose and pectin in its cell walls is collenchyma.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q14 - Absence of fibres in conifer secondary xylem

questiontext.text: In conifers fibres are likely to be absent in

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Conifers (gymnosperms) have a simpler xylem anatomy compared to angiosperms.

Step 2: Evaluation of Conifer Tissues
The secondary xylem of conifers (softwood) is composed almost entirely of tracheids and xylem parenchyma (rays), and it characteristically lacks both vessels and true wood fibres (sclerenchyma fibres). In contrast, phloem fibres and sclerenchymatous hypodermal/mechanical fibres in leaves can be present in conifers.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In conifers, fibres are likely to be absent in the secondary xylem.

questiontext.text: When we peel the skin of a potato tuber, we remove

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A potato tuber is an underground modified stem (a dicot stem) that undergoes secondary thickening in the outer cortical region.

Step 2: Evaluation of Tuber Structure
As the potato tuber enlarges, the original epidermis and cuticle are replaced by a protective periderm (comprising phellem/cork, phellogen/cork cambium, and phelloderm). This outer corky skin is what is peeled away. Sapwood is secondary xylem found inside the vascular cambium of woody trunks, not on the outer surface of a potato tuber.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
When we peel the skin of a potato tuber, we remove the periderm.

questiontext.text: A vesselless piece of stem possessing prominent sieve tubes would belong to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Typically, angiosperms possess both xylem vessels and phloem sieve tubes (with companion cells), whereas gymnosperms lack vessels and possess sieve cells rather than sieve tubes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Exceptional Taxa
Pinus is a gymnosperm, so it lacks both vessels and sieve tubes. Eucalyptus and grasses are typical angiosperms that possess vessels as well as sieve tubes. Trochodendron is an exceptional primitive angiosperm whose wood is vesselless (lacking tracheae), yet its phloem possesses prominent sieve tubes characteristic of angiosperms.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A vesselless piece of stem possessing prominent sieve tubes belongs to Trochodendron.

questiontext.text: Which one of the following cell types always divides by anticlinal cell division?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Anticlinal cell division occurs perpendicular to the surface of the plant organ, increasing the surface area of a layer without increasing the number of cell layers. Periclinal division occurs parallel to the surface, adding new layers in thickness.

Step 2: Evaluation of Cell Types
The protoderm is the outermost primary meristematic layer that gives rise to the uniseriate (single-layered) epidermis; therefore, its cells always divide anticlinally to keep pace with internal growth while remaining a single layer. In contrast, phellogen, fusiform initials, and root cap initials undergo periclinal divisions (as well as anticlinal divisions) to produce multiple layers of cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The cell type that always divides by anticlinal cell division is protoderm.

name.text: NCERTEXEMPLAR_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q18 - Fate of primary xylem in dicot root

questiontext.text: What is the fate of primary xylem in a dicot root showing extensive secondary growth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a dicot root, the vascular cambium forms as a wavy ring located between the primary xylem (towards the centre) and primary phloem (towards the periphery), and it cuts off secondary xylem towards the inside and secondary phloem towards the outside.

Step 2: Evaluation of Secondary Growth
As the vascular cambium produces abundant secondary xylem internally and secondary phloem externally, the older primary phloem is pushed outward and eventually crushed. However, the primary xylem lies at the very centre of the root axis inside the ring of secondary xylem, and its lignified walls resist compression, so it remains intact at the centre of the axis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In a dicot root showing extensive secondary growth, the primary xylem is retained in the centre of the axis.

answer.text: It is retained in the centre of the axis
